steps.prompt: Before anything is explained: why do you think Black pushed that pawn, and what would you do as White? Write one line. There is no wrong answer yet.

steps.caption: Watch what happens if White does not notice the pawn.

line.say: White makes an unrelated move and ignores the pawn.
The pawn takes the knight, and no white piece can take back.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 is attacked and nothing defends it.
If White passes, Black comes out at least two points ahead.

steps.caption: The same position, but now White does notice and answers the threat.

line.say: The knight steps to a square the pawn does not attack.
Black has nothing to take, so the threat has gone.

claims.statement: No black piece attacks the knight on b3.

steps.text: A **threat** is the strongest thing your opponent could start with their *next* move if you did nothing: win something loose, give checkmate, or attack two pieces at once. It can be a short forcing line, not only one capture. Ask it after **every** opponent move, before your own plan. Why: your plan was made for the position before their move, and their move is the only new fact, so look there first. [H] I think skipping this look causes many club blunders; I have not measured it.

steps.caption: Black to move. Watch the rook's last move, and what it makes possible.

line.say: The rook moves to the c-file. Look at where it now points.
White plays an unrelated move and does not look.
The rook slides down the file and takes the bishop. Nothing takes back.

claims.statement: After the rook move the bishop on c3 is attacked and undefended.
No white piece defends the bishop on c3.

steps.caption: Same position, White to move. This time White checks what Black's last move attacked.

line.say: The bishop leaves the c-file for a square nothing attacks.
The rook has nothing left to take.

claims.statement: After the bishop moves no white piece is attacked and undefended.

steps.text: After each opponent move, look at four things. **Where did the moved piece go, and what does it attack now?** **What line did it open?** A piece that steps aside can unmask one behind it. **Is any piece of mine loose?** Attacked and undefended: check it first. **Does it give check or pin something?** A pinned piece cannot move freely. With two threats at once, look for one move that answers both, such as capturing the attacker.

steps.caption: Black to move. A bishop is about to step aside, and the rook behind it is the real danger.

line.say: The bishop steps off the e-file. It attacks nothing important, but it uncovers the rook.
White plays on without checking what the last move opened.
The rook runs down the open file and takes the undefended knight.

claims.statement: After the bishop moves the knight on e2 is attacked and undefended.
While the bishop stands on e6 nothing attacks the knight.

steps.caption: Same position, White to move. White sees the uncovered rook and answers it.

line.say: The knight leaves the e-file and goes where the rook cannot reach it.
Black has nothing to take.

claims.statement: Before the knight moves, it is attacked and undefended.
After the knight moves nothing is attacked and undefended.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's bishop pins the knight to the king, and a pawn also attacks it. A pinned piece cannot step away.

line.say: White makes an unrelated move.
The pawn takes the pinned knight, which could not leave.

claims.statement: The pinned knight has no legal move.
A black pawn attacks the knight.
If White passes, Black comes out ahead.

steps.text: Three kinds of threat come up again and again. You have met the first: **winning a piece** that is loose. The second is **checkmate**. The third is **attacking two things with one move**, such as your king and a piece, so that you can only save one. People call that last one a **fork**.

steps.caption: Black to move. White has just put a rook on the open e-file. Is it a threat?

line.say: Black ignores the rook and plays an unrelated move.
The rook lands on e8 with check. The pawns shut the king in and nothing covers e8: checkmate.

claims.statement: White threatens Re8 checkmate.
No black piece covers e8.

steps.caption: Black spotted the threat and played a pawn move. Does the same rook move still mate?

line.say: The rook still gives check on e8.
But the king walks to h7, the square the pawn move gave it. No mate.

claims.statement: Re8 is check but not checkmate.
The square h7 is empty, so the king can go there.

steps.text: A piece standing **behind** another on the same line backs it up. A queen with a bishop behind it on a diagonal is guarded through the queen: if the queen captures, the bishop covers that square. That can turn a capture the king could answer into one it cannot. [I] This idea sits behind many mating threats against a castled king.

steps.caption: White to move. The queen and bishop line up towards h2. Is that a threat?

line.say: White plays an unrelated move.
The queen takes h2 with check. The bishop behind it guards the square, and the rook blocks the king's last exit: checkmate.

claims.statement: If White passes, Qxh2 is checkmate.
Only the king guards h2.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's knight has just jumped to d4. Nothing of White's is attacked yet.

line.say: White sees nothing attacked and plays an unrelated move.
The knight jumps to e2 with check. From there it also attacks the rook.
White must answer the check first, so the rook cannot be saved.
The knight takes the rook.

claims.statement: No white piece is attacked right now.
No white piece covers e2.
From e2 the knight attacks both the king on g1 and the rook on c1.
If White passes, the knight wins the rook.

steps.caption: Black to move. White spotted the jump and put the rook where it covers e2.

line.say: Black tries the fork anyway.
The rook covers e2 and simply takes the knight.

claims.statement: The rook on e1 covers e2.
Ne2 just loses the knight.

steps.text: Eugene Znosko-Borovsky, in *The Middle Game in Chess* (1922), split threats into direct ones, which act at once, and distant ones, which show only over several moves, and said the decisive role belongs to the distant ones. [I] My reading: a fork is a direct threat, so the distant kind is what later lessons train.

steps.caption: White to move. One pawn move has attacked two knights at once.

line.say: White plays an unrelated move.
The pawn takes one knight.
White saves the other knight, but a piece is gone.

claims.statement: A black pawn attacks the knight on c4.
The same pawn attacks the knight on e4.
If White passes, Black wins a knight.

steps.text: **Remember.** A threat is the strongest thing your opponent could start next if you did nothing. After every opponent move, ask where the moved piece went, what line it opened, whether any of your pieces is loose, and whether it gives check or pins. Look before you follow your own plan.
